#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when a library has multiple flavours*
This scenario demonstrates selecting a specific published flavour of a library. With a plain Maven repository that means a classifier; with Gradle Module Metadata it becomes attribute-based variant selection.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **Gradle 8.14**.
Re-verified on Gradle 9.3 (October 2026): Gradle 9 raised the runtime floor to JDK 17 and changed defaults such as the configuration cache, not the resolution rules shown here.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> LibA[lib-a:1.0.0]
    LibA --> Jar["lib-a-1.0.0.jar"]
    LibA --> Jdk11["lib-a-1.0.0-jdk11.jar (classifier)"]
    Root -. selects .-> Jdk11
```

`lib-a:1.0.0` is published twice in the demo repository: the default jar and a `jdk11` classifier. We pick the classifier explicitly:

```{.groovy include="build.gradle" snippet="s13-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
Gradle works out which flavour of `lib-a` suits the project from the JDK it compiles against, so the `jdk11` build arrives automatically.

#### ! Actual
Nothing is automatic here. The dependency tree prints `com.demo:lib-a:1.0.0` with no sign of the classifier at all; only the resolved *files* reveal that `lib-a-1.0.0-jdk11.jar` was selected, and only because the build named it. Drop the `:jdk11` and the plain jar comes back. A classifier is an artifact name, not a property Gradle can reason about.

#### ! Why
Gradle's dependency model has two layers. A *component* (`com.demo:lib-a:1.0.0`) has *variants*, each described by attributes (`org.gradle.usage`, `org.gradle.jvm.version`, ...) and capabilities, and Gradle selects a variant by matching the consumer's requested attributes against them. That selection is automatic, but it needs the producer to publish variants, which means Gradle Module Metadata (`.module` files). A library published with a POM alone has one variant per scope and no attributes beyond the defaults; its classifiers are just extra files hanging off the component, invisible to matching. For such libraries you select the file by name, exactly as Maven does. The `dependencyInsight` report shows the attributes Gradle *requested* (including `org.gradle.jvm.version`), which is what a producer with real variants would match against.

#### ! Fix
*   **POM-only library:** request the classifier, `'com.demo:lib-a:1.0.0:jdk11'`, and accept that nothing checks it matches your JDK.
*   **Library with Gradle Module Metadata:** declare the plain coordinates and let attribute matching choose; override only with `attributes { ... }` on the dependency when the default request is wrong.
*   **You are the producer:** publish with the `maven-publish` plugin (which emits `.module` metadata) and expose flavours as variants or feature variants ([GS8](../scenario-8-optional/guide.qmd)), so consumers stop hard-coding classifiers.

#### ! Risk
* LOW A classifier for a well-understood artifact such as `sources` or `javadoc`.
* MEDIUM A classifier chosen for the JDK or platform that nobody updates when the project moves on, so the build keeps shipping the old flavour.
* HIGH Two classifiers of the same component on one classpath (one requested directly, one through a transitive), both resolving to `lib-a:1.0.0` in the tree and duplicating every class.

#### ! Control
*   **Check the files, not the tree,** when classifiers are involved: a task that prints `configurations.runtimeClasspath.files` (the demo's `printRuntimeJars`) shows which jar actually resolved.
*   **Read `outgoingVariants` and `resolvableConfigurations`** to see the attributes in play when matching errors appear ("Cannot choose between", "No matching variant found").

#### ! Check
**Fast check:**

```bash
gradle printRuntimeJars
gradle dependencies --configuration compileClasspath
```

**What to look for:** `JAR lib-a-1.0.0-jdk11.jar` from the first command; `com.demo:lib-a:1.0.0` with no classifier mentioned in the second.

**Conclusion:** The classifier selected a file; the dependency graph is unchanged and unaware.

#### ! Scales
Attribute-based variants are how the JVM ecosystem is moving beyond classifiers: a producer can publish JDK-specific, platform-specific or feature-specific variants and let every consumer's build select the right one without naming it. Until a library publishes Gradle Module Metadata, though, its consumers are back to classifiers, and the mismatch between the two models (one automatic, one manual) is a frequent source of confusion in mixed builds.

#### ! Takeaway
Classifiers pick a file by name and Gradle cannot see what they mean; variants pick by attributes and Gradle matches them for you. Which one you get depends on what the producer published.

#### ! Wild

Guava is the best-known library to make the jump. For years it shipped two flavours as classifiers and separate version suffixes (`-jre` and `-android`), and consumers had to pick by name. Since Guava 32 it also publishes Gradle Module Metadata declaring both as variants of one component, selected by the `org.gradle.jvm.environment` attribute: a Gradle build targeting the standard JVM gets the `-jre` flavour and an Android build the `-android` one, from the same coordinates. Maven consumers still choose a suffix by hand, which is a neat illustration of the two models living side by side on the same artifact.
